question: For an unweighted average of similarly distributed predictors, when does expected loss improve monotonically as ensemble size grows, and how do convexity, local curvature, dependence, and classification ties change the answer?

key_findings.claim: For a convex loss and exchangeable predictions, expected loss is non-increasing with every added ensemble member.
key_findings.evidence: The paper writes the K-member mean as the average of all K leave-one-out means. Convexity bounds its loss by the average leave-one-out loss, and exchangeability makes every expected leave-one-out term equal to the expected loss of the first K-1 members. The result is pointwise in the prediction problem and extends to a dataset only when the reported metric is an average of such losses.

key_findings.claim: Strong convexity yields an explicit strict-improvement lower bound controlled by prediction variance and dependence.
key_findings.evidence: For an exchangeable ensemble with covariance Sigma and trace-correlation rho, Theorem 4 subtracts mu(1-rho)tr(Sigma)/(K(K-1)) from the K-1-member expected loss. The appendix derives this with a strengthened Jensen inequality and covariance algebra. Independent members have rho=0, while identical copies have rho=1 and no guaranteed gain.

key_findings.claim: For a smooth nonconvex loss, sufficiently large i.i.d. ensembles improve at a locally convex asymptotic prediction and worsen at a locally concave one.
key_findings.evidence: Theorem 5 assumes nondegenerate i.i.d. predictions with five finite moments and a loss with bounded continuous derivatives through order five. A fourth-order delta expansion makes the eventual K-to-K+1 difference have the sign of tr(H(y-infinity)Sigma), so a positive-definite Hessian gives improvement and a negative-definite Hessian gives deterioration. The claim does not cover inflection points or indefinite Hessians.

key_findings.claim: The univariate tail theorem gives a useful but highly regular eventual-monotonicity result and explains why ordinary Bernoulli voting can oscillate.
key_findings.evidence: Theorem 7 proves eventual strict decrease of both weak and strict upper-tail probabilities when the moment-generating function is finite on all real arguments, the tail is nonempty, and the summand is either absolutely continuous or lattice-valued with mass exactly at the threshold. Petrov's sharp large-deviation expansion makes the consecutive-tail ratio converge below one. A Bernoulli threshold generally misses the lattice, producing the odd/even tie oscillation shown in Figure 8.

key_findings.claim: The classification-error result is credible in its binary route but its multiclass route inherits the multivariate theorem's proof defect.
key_findings.evidence: Lemma 6 rewrites error as an orthant-tail probability of correct-versus-incorrect margins. For two classes, Theorem 10 can invoke the independently proved univariate Theorem 7. For more than two classes it instead invokes Theorem 8; the positive result additionally requires every expected margin to be positive, while the negative result requires the true class to have lower asymptotic score than every wrong class, not merely to lose the argmax.

key_findings.claim: The published proof does not establish the stated multivariate monotonicity theorem.
key_findings.evidence: Theorem 8 assumes min_i epsilon_i/||epsilon|| < sqrt(lambda_min/lambda_max), but its proof immediately invokes Lemma 15, which instead requires min_i epsilon_i/||epsilon|| > sqrt(2(1-sqrt(lambda_min/lambda_max))) plus a full moment-domain and support-interior condition absent from Theorem 8. Remark 16 says that lemma condition may require near-isotropy, contradicting the theorem discussion that an arbitrarily small coordinate suffices. The proof also prints the rate as tau^T a-varphi(a) rather than tau^T a-varphi(tau), and equation 54 drops the nth power from phi_n(t)=phi(t)^n while using that missing power to claim decay. These are structural, not cosmetic, gaps in the route used for multiclass classification.

key_findings.claim: The slogan that monotonic improvement holds if and only if the loss is convex is broader than the formal results supplied.
key_findings.evidence: Theorem 2 proves convexity is sufficient under exchangeability, and the nonconvex section gives local sufficient conditions for eventual improvement or deterioration under stronger i.i.d. assumptions. The paper does not state or prove a converse theorem showing that every nonconvex loss fails universal monotonicity under a specified ensemble class. The slogan is defensible as an informal universal-guarantee heuristic, but not as a proved biconditional without extra regularity and quantifiers.

key_findings.claim: The paper's practical recommendation to make ensembles as large as feasible is partly heuristic and requires exchangeability and metric qualifications.
key_findings.evidence: Section 6.1 says this is always true for convex losses and likely true on aggregate for nonconvex losses because good points should outnumber bad ones. The proved convex statement concerns expected loss under exchangeable members; adding an intentionally weak or order-dependent member can hurt. The nonconvex dataset-level claim is not a theorem, and no compute-normalized stopping rule is analyzed despite diminishing O(1/K) gains in the expansions.

key_findings.claim: The dermatology plots illustrate the predicted shapes but do not constitute a reproducible or assumption-checked test of the theorems.
key_findings.evidence: A single described LeNet-like model with 50% dropout is evaluated on binary DermaMNIST splits of 1,548/221/443 images. Figures 1-4 average curves over 500 repetitions: cross-entropy decreases, sigmoid loss decreases on asymptotically correct images and increases on incorrect ones, and accuracy separates similarly. Figure 5 adds basal-cell carcinoma and shows a four-way multiclass split. The exact architecture, optimizer, epochs, seed, weights, asymptotic-prediction approximation, and theorem regularity checks are not reported, and the linked repository contains none of this experiment.

key_findings.claim: The movie-rating experiment matches the local-curvature predictions for six selected movies, including delayed eventual worsening near an inflection point.
key_findings.evidence: For each of 20 films the paper samples K=1,...,50 ratings with replacement and repeats 10,000 times. The artifact data reproduce absolute crowd-mean errors of 28.845 for John Wick 2, 5.409 for Ghost in the Shell, 14.922 for Beauty and the Beast, 31.731 for Logan, 0.364 for The Space Between Us, and 13.801 for Smurfs. Squared loss decreases; Welsch and Geman-McClure losses decrease below the chosen error threshold 10 and eventually increase above it. These are six displayed selections, not an aggregate success rate over all 20 films.

key_findings.claim: The interpretation of the Appendix G delta expansion reverses what its leading term says about convergence magnitude.
key_findings.evidence: Equation 59 gives E[L(y_K)]-L(y_infinity)=L''(y-infinity)Var(y_1)/(2K)+O(K^-3/2). The text says this means convergence is slower when the second derivative is small. At fixed K, a smaller leading coefficient instead makes the loss closer to its limit; what can become slower is the onset of the eventual monotonic sign when higher-order terms dominate near an inflection point. The empirical delayed reversal is real, but the displayed expansion does not support the stated convergence-speed explanation.

key_findings.claim: The released artifact partially reproduces the crowd plots but is not a complete or exact reproduction package.
key_findings.evidence: GitHub commit 5e2264319d6f21cb53e27ab80b0cdea46b2540a8 contains one executed notebook and 20 crowd-rating files. It has no medical experiment, dependency lock, random seed, saved figure source, test suite, or environment instructions. The notebook's unseeded 10,000-repetition simulation reconstructs the movie setup and stored outputs, but exact reruns vary; one filter uses df_w to index df_gm and one Welsch plot is mislabeled Geman-McClure. The six paper values computed directly from the bundled ratings do match.

method.core_idea: Reduce ensemble-size monotonicity to geometry of the loss at averages: global convexity gives a leave-one-out Jensen inequality, while local curvature or sharp tail asymptotics governs eventual behavior for nonconvex losses.
method.mechanism: The convex result averages all leave-one-out subensembles and uses exchangeability. Strong convexity adds a variance-correlation improvement term. Smooth nonconvex losses are expanded to fourth order around the infinite-ensemble mean. Classification error is rewritten as a tail probability of mean margin vectors and analyzed with univariate or multivariate strong large deviations. Dropout and crowd experiments visualize the resulting decreasing or increasing curves.
assumptions: Aggregation is an unweighted arithmetic mean in a convex prediction set.
Convex-loss monotonicity requires exchangeable ensemble members and finite expected losses.
Strict quantitative improvement requires strong convexity, second moments, nonzero variance, and dependence below perfect correlation.
Smooth nonconvex results require nondegenerate i.i.d. predictions with five moments and bounded continuous loss derivatives through order five.
Binary classification monotonicity requires strong moment-generating and continuity or lattice-threshold conditions on the margin.
The multiclass route additionally needs an orthant-tail theorem with a positive exponential tilt; the published theorem does not state the conditions its proof uses.
Dataset-level transfer applies directly only to metrics that are arithmetic averages of pointwise losses.
The experiments treat finite Monte Carlo approximations as proxies for asymptotic predictions and do not verify all distributional assumptions.

techniques.role: Expresses a K-member mean as the average of all K subensembles of size K-1.
Makes the expected losses of all leave-one-out subensembles identical without requiring independence.
Converts ensemble variance and pairwise dependence into an explicit strict-improvement term.
Uses fourth-order moment expansions to determine eventual monotonicity for smooth nonconvex losses.
Rewrites classification error as an upper-tail probability of averaged correct-class margins.
Uses sharp Petrov and Joutard asymptotics to seek consecutive-size tail ratios below one.
Generates exchangeable test-time neural predictions from independent dropout masks.
Forms synthetic ensembles by resampling human movie-rating forecasts with replacement.

evaluations.setting: Any exchangeable ensemble evaluated pointwise with a convex loss
evaluations.metric: Expected loss at K versus K-1 members
evaluations.result: Non-increasing for every K by Theorem 2
evaluations.baseline: A single member or the preceding K-1-member ensemble

evaluations.setting: Exchangeable ensemble with a mu-strongly convex loss and second moments
evaluations.result: At least mu(1-rho)tr(Sigma)/(K(K-1)) under the paper's strong-convexity convention

evaluations.setting: Smooth nonconvex loss with nondegenerate i.i.d. predictions
evaluations.metric: Eventual sign of the K-to-K+1 expected-loss difference
evaluations.result: Improves at a positive-definite Hessian and worsens at a negative-definite Hessian
evaluations.baseline: No conclusion at an inflection point or indefinite Hessian

evaluations.setting: Binary and multiclass classification by averaged score vectors
evaluations.result: Binary claim follows under Theorem 7's margin conditions; the multiclass proof depends on the unestablished Theorem 8
evaluations.baseline: Bernoulli majority voting, where odd/even ties break monotonicity

evaluations.setting: Binary DermaMNIST; 1,548 training, 221 validation, and 443 test images; one LeNet-like model with 50% dropout
evaluations.metric: Accuracy, cross-entropy, and sigmoid loss versus ensemble size over 500 repetitions
evaluations.result: Convex cross-entropy curves decrease; accuracy and sigmoid loss improve on asymptotically correct points and worsen on incorrect points
evaluations.baseline: The same fixed network under fewer sampled dropout masks

evaluations.setting: Three-class DermaMNIST variant adding basal-cell carcinoma
evaluations.metric: Accuracy versus ensemble size over 500 repetitions, stratified by asymptotic prediction status
evaluations.result: Accuracy improves for correct points and degrades for completely incorrect points; intermediate incorrect points also degrade empirically

evaluations.setting: Twenty upcoming-movie crowd forecasts; K=1 to 50; 10,000 resamples with replacement per K
evaluations.result: Six displayed films follow the predicted convex decrease or eventual local-concavity increase; Smurfs reverses only after an initial decrease

evaluations.metric: Coverage and exact reproducibility of Figures 1-6 and 10
evaluations.result: Bundled data and notebook support the movie figures and exact crowd means, but medical code is absent and unseeded dependencies prevent exact reruns
evaluations.baseline: A complete pinned package for both experiments

limitations: Author-stated: only unweighted arithmetic averaging is analyzed; other aggregation rules are left open.
Author-stated: the results concern mean loss, not the full loss distribution or algorithmic variance.
Author-stated: direct dataset aggregation does not cover AUC, median squared error, calibration, or other non-average metrics.
Author-stated: multiclass predictions that are wrong but not completely wrong fall outside the negative half of Theorem 10.
Reviewer-identified: Theorem 8's epsilon condition, domain assumptions, and proof do not match Lemma 15, leaving the multiclass classification theorem unsupported as written.
Reviewer-identified: equation 54 omits the nth power needed for its decay argument, and the multivariate rate expression substitutes varphi(a) for varphi(tau).
Reviewer-identified: the abstract's if-and-only-if slogan is not supplied as a converse theorem with explicit quantifiers and regularity.
Reviewer-identified: the practical large-as-feasible recommendation is heuristic for nonconvex losses and omits compute-normalized marginal utility.
Reviewer-identified: the medical experiment has no released code, exact model specification, weights, seeds, or environment and does not check theorem assumptions.
Reviewer-identified: the movie artifact is unseeded and unpinned, displays only six selected films, and contains minor filtering and labeling defects.
Reviewer-identified: Figure 3's caption says the frontier separates a concave part from a concave part, and the paper alternates Welsh and Welsch spellings.
Reviewer-identified: Appendix G's claim that a smaller second derivative means slower convergence is opposite to the magnitude of its displayed leading 1/K term.
failure_modes: A non-exchangeable sequence can worsen when a correlated duplicate or systematically weaker model is appended.
Classification ties can create persistent odd/even oscillations even for i.i.d. Bernoulli voters.
A heavy-tailed summand without a finite mean can make upper-tail probability increase with sample size.
At an inflection point or with an indefinite Hessian, the smooth-loss theorem gives no eventual direction.
For multiclass scores, some negative margins and some positive margins satisfy neither the correct nor completely incorrect condition.
If the required positive exponential tilt does not exist, the orthant large-deviation formula and the multiclass conclusion fail.
Pointwise improvements and deteriorations can cancel non-monotonically in a dataset-level nonconvex metric.
Unseeded Monte Carlo plots can look locally non-monotone because sampling error is larger than a small theoretical K-to-K+1 change.
reusable_insights: Prove ensemble-size monotonicity with leave-one-out symmetrization before reaching for asymptotics.
State whether a claim concerns a point, a dataset average, expectation over model randomness, or a realized trained ensemble.
Separate a universal convex guarantee from eventual local-curvature behavior for nonconvex metrics.
Treat ties and lattice alignment as first-class design choices in voting systems.
For multiclass majority decisions, inspect the full margin vector and whether the saddlepoint tilt lies in the positive orthant.
Report convex and nonconvex metrics together because likelihood improvement need not imply accuracy or perceptual-metric improvement.
Balance marginal expected gain against inference cost instead of interpreting monotonicity as an unlimited-size prescription.
Release exact seeds, model checkpoints, environments, and all displayed experiment code even when results are illustrative.
open_questions: What is a correct minimal condition for multivariate orthant-tail monotonicity, and does it recover the intended multiclass theorem?
Can the necessity direction of the convexity slogan be stated and proved for a precise class of continuous losses and exchangeable ensembles?
What happens for weighted, geometric, trimmed, median, or learned aggregation as members are added?
Can eventual monotonicity thresholds K0 be bounded in observable quantities rather than left asymptotic?
How should ensemble size be selected under joint accuracy, calibration, latency, energy, and memory costs?
When does a dataset mixture of improving and worsening points remain monotone for a nonconvex metric?
Can analogous results cover AUC, FID, calibration error, and other metrics that are not pointwise averages?
Do the dermatology curves replicate across architectures, training seeds, dropout rates, and medical datasets with all assumptions checked?

competitive_landscape.title: To tune or not to tune the number of trees in random forest?
competitive_landscape.difference: Probst and Boulesteix already show theoretically and across 306 OpenML datasets that Brier, log, and squared losses avoid the classification-error nonmonotonicity seen as tree count grows. The reviewed paper lifts those metric-specific observations to a general exchangeable convex-loss theorem and adds local nonconvex and tail analyses.

competitive_landscape.title: Estimating a sharp convergence bound for randomized ensembles
competitive_landscape.difference: Lopes quantifies stabilization of majority-vote error through sharp algorithmic-variance bounds and estimators, whereas the reviewed work targets the sign of every or eventual K-to-K+1 change. The reviewed paper correctly notes that low-order convergence expansions alone do not imply monotonicity.

competitive_landscape.title: Uphill Roads to Variational Tightness: Monotonicity and Monte Carlo Objectives
competitive_landscape.difference: Mattei and Frellsen study monotone tightening of Monte Carlo objectives, correlation, and nonuniform weights using stochastic orders. The reviewed paper transfers the leave-one-out convexity logic to predictive ensembles and develops nonconvex loss and classification-tail cases.

competitive_landscape.title: When are ensembles really effective?
competitive_landscape.difference: Theisen et al. bound relative classification improvement through disagreement versus error and test interpolating and non-interpolating models. The reviewed paper instead asks monotonicity with ensemble size across arbitrary convex losses and supplies local-curvature conditions, but has much narrower empirical coverage.

competitive_landscape.title: When Are Two Scores Better Than One? Investigating Ensembles of Diffusion Models
competitive_landscape.difference: This follow-up shows that score ensembling can improve convex score-matching loss and likelihood without consistently improving nonconvex perceptual quality such as FID, directly extending the reviewed paper's metric-dependence message beyond supervised prediction.

competitive_landscape.title: Beyond Mixtures and Products for Ensemble Aggregation: A Likelihood Perspective on Generalized Means
competitive_landscape.difference: The follow-up moves beyond arithmetic means to normalized generalized means and identifies r in [0,1] as the range with systematic log-likelihood improvement over individuals. It addresses an aggregation question explicitly left open here, while focusing on improvement over members rather than consecutive-size monotonicity.

novelty_assessment.author_claim: The paper claims a unified convexity-based answer to whether unweighted ensembles improve with every added member, strict gains under strong convexity, eventual local-curvature laws for smooth nonconvex losses, and new univariate and multivariate tail-monotonicity theorems supporting classification error.
novelty_assessment.evidence: The final JMLR version contains a short exchangeable leave-one-out proof, an explicit variance-correlation bound, a fourth-order delta proof, Petrov-based univariate tail ratios, a proposed Joutard-based multivariate extension, and dropout and crowd illustrations. The linked artifact supports only the crowd experiment.
novelty_assessment.reviewer_inference: The cleanest contribution is the general pointwise convex-loss formulation and its synthesis of older majorization, Monte Carlo, and random-forest results; the smooth local-curvature theorem is also useful. Prior work already covered metric-specific random-forest monotonicity, majority-vote rates, Monte Carlo-objective monotonicity, and diversity-based ensemble gains. The new multivariate tail result is not established by the printed proof because its theorem and key lemma impose incompatible conditions and the large-deviation verification contains missing factors. Consequently the binary classification contribution is stronger than the multiclass headline, and the if-and-only-if and large-as-feasible language should be read as qualified heuristics. Later same-author work broadens the metric and aggregation picture to diffusion-model quality and generalized means.

reviewer_notes: Primary full-text review of the exact cached arXiv:2311.17885v3 / final JMLR 26(201) artifact. I read all 46 pages, every theorem, proof, displayed equation, reference, and caption, and visually inspected all ten figures including the Appendix F geometry. I also inspected the complete submitted TeX source and every bundled source figure. The PDF and text hashes and 46-page count match the indexed provenance; the official arXiv record identifies v3 dated 2025-12-30 and the JMLR page identifies the 2025 final publication. The linked GitHub repository was audited at commit 5e2264319d6f21cb53e27ab80b0cdea46b2540a8; its notebook and all 20 data files were inspected, Python syntax was checked, and the six displayed crowd-mean errors were independently recomputed. Six exact-version primary competitors or follow-ups were checked through 2026-08-24. Confidence is high for the convex, smooth-loss, univariate-tail, artifact, and empirical-boundary findings; it is intentionally lower for the truth of a potentially repairable multivariate theorem beyond the fact that the published proof does not establish its stated version.
